summary:
Oman is a destination trans and gender-nonconforming travellers should avoid. The Penal Law (Royal Decree 7/2018) criminalises same-sex conduct with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, and its provisions on impersonation and gender non-conformity reach presentation as well as acts. The Public Prosecution has stated that any male who appears in female clothing or demeanour may be fined up to OMR 3,000 and jailed for up to one year, with additional charges available for publishing such material on social media. These provisions are applied to foreign nationals.

The statute set is broad. Article 265 covers public indecency (10 days to 3 months plus an OMR 100–300 fine); Article 266 covers impersonation and entry into women-only venues while disguised (1 month to 1 year); Articles 267 and 268 cover producing or sharing content held to violate public morals, offline and online (up to 1 year, or 10 days to 1 month). Gender non-conformity is punished through Article 266(d). The 2011 Cyber Crime Law, Articles 17 and 31, has been used against LGBT expression, carrying 1 month to 3 years plus an OMR 100–3,000 fine.

Enforcement against gender presentation is documented rather than theoretical. In January 2018 the Royal Oman Police announced the arrest of a group of men for dressing as women after photographs circulated on social media; Human Rights Watch wrote to Oman's authorities in an open letter of 13 July 2020 about arrests and convictions under the Penal Code's cross-dressing provision, including arrests of men in women's clothing after Snapchat photos from a private party in Salalah and the arrest of an Asian expatriate wearing an abaya and niqab during a women-only hour at a park in Al Buraimi.

Courts have imposed custodial sentences. A Salalah preliminary court sentenced two men to four years' imprisonment and OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and sharing photographs of themselves in women's clothing on social media, and sentenced two further men to three years with the same fine for appearing in the video, with additional charges for publishing immoral acts on social media.

At the border, a genderqueer non-binary Indian model and activist arriving at Muscat International Airport on a 10-day tourist visa on 27 February 2023 reported that friends cleared immigration while she was held for separate examination, made to remove her shirt, and touched inappropriately by officers. That is direct first-hand evidence of how a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor can be treated on arrival, alongside refusal of entry.

Prosecution does not require a complaint from family. Cases are often triggered by digital evidence surfaced during unrelated investigations, and Oman's Article 49 exception removes the usual dual-criminality protection, so conduct abroad can still be pursued. Article 60 requires deportation of foreign nationals convicted of a felony (permanent exclusion) and permits it for misdemeanours (3–15 years). The state ISP enables surveillance, and outing a person carries both social and criminal consequences.
tangentialFactors:
Cairo 52 and White Tent's joint stakeholder submission of 6 August 2025 to Oman's fourth-cycle Universal Periodic Review documents systemic legal and institutional discrimination against transgender people, states that recent legislative developments have deepened the criminalisation of gender expression, and reports that Oman ignored earlier UPR recommendations on gender identity, expression and health access. The submission recommends ending criminalisation, adopting anti-discrimination legislation, and permitting legal recognition.

Regional comparison places Oman's cross-dressing offence alongside Kuwait's 2007 imitation law. Human Rights Watch's regional report of 16 April 2018 records that Oman's 2018 Penal Code added a provision punishing any man who appears to dress in women's clothing, on top of pre-existing criminalisation of same-sex conduct and documented barriers to LGBT organising.

Restrictions on assembly and advocacy under the Civil Associations Law narrow the space in which a visitor's local contacts could offer support or complain on their behalf.
localsOnly:
Oman bans legal gender recognition and explicitly bans gender-affirming healthcare, according to the August 2025 UPR submission by Cairo 52 and White Tent. Residents therefore have no lawful route to align identity documents with presentation, and cannot obtain transition-related care in-country.

Residents live under the same cross-dressing and public-morals provisions described for visitors, with prosecution reachable through social-media material and digital evidence gathered in unrelated investigations, and with no family-complaint requirement. The 2011 Cyber Crime Law extends liability to online posting.

Advocacy and organising are constrained by the Civil Associations Law, and Human Rights Watch has recorded barriers to LGBT organising in its regional reporting. Anti-discrimination legislation remains absent, a gap the UPR submission explicitly asks the government to close.

Foreign residents convicted of a felony face permanent deportation under Article 60, while misdemeanour convictions can trigger deportation after a 3–15 year period.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile at humandignitytrust.org/country-profile/oman/ returned HTTP 403 at research time and could not be read directly; its content on criminalisation of same-sex activity and gender expression is described second-hand in the inventory and is not independently verified here.

Reported article numbering for the cross-dressing offence is inconsistent across sources: the 2018 Penal Code provision is cited as Article 266(d) in statute-level extraction and as Article 22 in coverage of the Public Prosecution's announcement. Which numbering appears in the operative text is unresolved.

The date of the Muscat airport examination is unresolved. The source inventory dates the account to 27 February 2023; other references to the same incident give February 2024.

No source states where inside the prison system people convicted of the cross-dressing offence were housed, including whether they were held in facilities matching their gender presentation. This remains unsourced.

The Shafiqa Ahmadi article on Islam and homosexuality offers general scholarly framing on the distinction between acts and identity but contains no Oman-specific or transgender-specific findings, and is not relied on for any claim above.
